title: Strive For a High Success Rate
author: Five Twelve Thirteen
summary: The author argues that a high student success rate on questions (80-90% correct) should be a teacher's operational benchmark, deliberately contrasted with a 'growth mindset' approach that encourages perseverance through work that is simply too hard. Rather than motivating students to push through consistently discouraging material, the teacher's job is to engineer conditions, through scaffolding, pacing, and curriculum modification, where most students succeed most of the time. The piece lists concrete downstream practices this benchmark drives: checking every student's response rather than a sample, adding review of prior learning, breaking concepts into smaller pieces when success rates lag, and treating a too-high success rate (consistently above 90%) as evidence the material is too easy. The author closes by stressing this is a ceiling as well as a floor, explicitly rejecting the reading that it means lowering expectations or avoiding challenge.
points: The author's key reframe: growth-mindset posters about perseverance often paper over curriculum that is simply too hard, whereas 'the primary job of the teacher is to engineer conditions where students are successful 80-90% of the time.'

A too-high success rate is itself a red flag, not just a too-low one: 'if the success rate is too high, consistently above 90%, then the curriculum is too easy,' making the benchmark a ceiling as well as a floor.
The success rate must be tracked per individual student, not in aggregate, since '80% of students get it right' at the class level can mask struggling students being quietly left behind.

The prioritization strategy trades curricular breadth for depth: the author cut other 7th-grade math content to focus disproportionately on equation solving, on the logic that a high success rate on the most essential skill beats shallow coverage of everything.
quotes: The primary job of the teacher is not to encourage students to persevere when things get hard. The primary job of the teacher is to engineer conditions where students are successful 80-90% of the time, inasmuch as that is possible.

A high success rate is my benchmark for whether a curriculum needs to be modified or supplemented. If students are not reaching a high success rate, I might need to add more scaffolding, adjust the sequencing, or make other changes.

Here's one thing that is not a high success rate: give students an exit ticket, 80% of students get it right, and say that's good enough and move on. The goal is that each individual student has a success rate of 80-90%.
My metric: if I'm struggling to get students to a high success rate, if we're practicing and they just aren't hitting that bar, I'm probably not breaking concepts down into small enough pieces.
The success rate I am striving for is a ceiling as much as a floor: a success rate of 100% is almost as bad as a success rate of 50%.
Teaching is an empirical science. Teaching is only effective if students learn something, if they can answer or produce something that they couldn't before.
